messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh was eighty years old, a retired data scientist who had spent two decades working for an international relief organization. In his mid-fifties, he had been deployed to a conflict zone, where his convoy was ambushed. He had been forced to watch as armed men executed two local colleagues, their bodies left in the road. Minh himself had been held at gunpoint for hours, certain he would be killed, before being released. He had never spoken of it in detail, not even to his late wife. Now, widowed and living alone, he found the past had begun to feel more present than the present itself.

The memory was not a recollection; it was a re-living. When Minh remembered the ambush, he felt the heat of the sun and the weight of the gun barrel against his temple. The scene played over and over, an unedited film he could not stop. He would wake from nightmares and lie still, the dream residue clinging to him, leaving him disoriented and afraid. The world, he had come to believe, was a dangerous place, and this conviction had seeped into everything. He was certain that if he did not control his anger, he would do something terrible, and that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy. These fears were not abstract; they were triggered by the smallest things. Seeing people misbehave—a driver cutting him off, a neighbor being rude—sent a spike of rage through him, and he would feel trapped, as if he had no options, no way out. A single news report about a conflict overseas could leave him shaking for hours. Each of these triggers made the memory surge back, vivid and immediate, and each time, the memory reinforced his belief that the world was irredeemably dangerous and that he was losing his grip.

To manage this, Minh had developed a set of strategies that consumed his days. He avoided all news reports about events similar to what had happened to him, which meant he had stopped watching television entirely. Before any interaction—a phone call with his daughter, a trip to the grocery store—he would rehearse what to say, running the conversation over and over in his mind, trying to anticipate every possible threat. He constantly scanned his environment for signs of danger, his body tense and ready to react. But these strategies backfired. Rehearsing conversations kept the trauma in his mind, making the memory feel more present. Scanning his environment meant he was always on the lookout for triggers, and he found them everywhere. A raised voice, a sudden movement, a person who reminded him of one of the gunmen—these would flood him with the memory of the ambush, and the cycle would begin again.

The more he avoided news, the more he isolated himself, and the more isolated he became, the more he felt the world pressing in. The belief that he was going crazy made him avoid people, and the avoidance made him feel more trapped, which in turn triggered the memory. The fear of his own rage made him rehearse conversations, but the rehearsal only reminded him of the helplessness he had felt in the war zone. His body was constantly on alert, and this physical tension itself became a trigger, a reminder that he was not safe.

He had stopped going to the grocery store. He had stopped answering the phone. His daughter, concerned, had begun leaving meals on his doorstep. What finally brought Minh to seek help was a morning when he woke from a nightmare and could not, for several minutes, remember where he was. He was terrified that he was losing his mind entirely. He was most afraid of what he might do if his anger ever broke through his careful control. But beneath that, he was hoping—though he could barely admit it—that someone could help him find a way to let the past be the past.
